title: Throughput claim audit: signals, sampling windows, and reproducibility checklist
content:
Purpose:
This note collects pragmatic guidance and a repeatable checklist for auditing throughput claims from the bench harness. The goal is to produce defensible throughput numbers that map to real production expectations (and to flag when numbers are fragile or likely inflated by sampling artifacts).

Context / Why this matters:
- We routinely get bench runs that claim X tokens/s but disagree with production telemetry. Small changes in sampling windows, client pacing, or observability aggregation explain a surprising fraction of mismatch.
- This doc focuses on the "audit" stage: after a benchmark run reports a figure, how do we validate it and what signals should we examine? It complements the harness design docs (load orchestration, warmup), but is intentionally signal-first.

Key signals to collect (minimum set):
1) Request-level latencies: p50/p90/p95/p99 (ms) and full histogram.
2) Server-side throughput by token: tokens emitted per second per worker process and per-GPU aggregate.
3) Client ingress rate: requests/sec arriving at the gateway (and distribution across clients).
4) Queue depth and wait time: number of in-flight requests and time spent waiting in queue before scheduling.
5) GPU utilization and SM clocks: GPU % util, memory bandwidth estimates, and clock throttle events.
6) Kernel-level counters: time in attention, decoding loop, KV cache ops when available.
7) OS and thermal events: CPU steal, temperature warnings, thermal throttling logs.
8) System-level wall-clock windows: what 60s/5m/15m window is being reported for throughput?
9) RNG/priming variance summary: seed usage and any priming/patch requests in the run.

Sampling windows and aggregation rules (recommended defaults):
- Warmup exclusion: drop the first N seconds (see warmup heuristics below). For our harness, default N = 120s for large models (>7B) and 60s for smaller models.
- Stable window selection: pick a contiguous 5-minute window with the lowest short-term variance (sliding 30s steps) after warmup to report the headline throughput. If the run is short (<6m) use the last 60% of the run after warmup.
- Reporting windows: always report 3 numbers -- Instantaneous peak (60s), Stable window median (5m), and Long-run average (15m) if available.
- Per-shard vs global: always publish both per-GPU (shard) throughput and global aggregate. Differences >5% indicate imbalance.

Warmup heuristics (quick checklist):
- Request prime: run a short priming phase that matches production request shapes (prefixes + full-length sequences) to fill caches.
- Adaptive warmup: monitor tokens/sec and p50 latency during warmup. Declare warm only after 3 consecutive 30s windows with <3% throughput delta and stable latency trend.
- Avoid single-shot priming spikes: interleave priming requests rather than a single heavy batch to avoid artificially inflating cache hit rates.

Reproducibility checks (post-run):
1) Replay at same RNG seeds and client distribution (if seeds used). If exact seeds are not available, run 3 independent seeds and report mean ± std.
2) Scale client concurrency up/down by ±10% to check robustness of the reported window.
3) Single-shard isolation: run the same workload pinned to a single GPU to measure per-shard behavior and compare to harness scaling model.
4) Noise injection: add small, controlled jitter (±5–10ms per-client delay) to detect sensitivity to inter-arrival regularity. If throughput drops >8%, document that the run depends on rigid pacing.

Common failure modes and how to detect them:
- Clock skew bias: if client and server clocks are misaligned, reported tokens/sec may be shifted. Detect by comparing server wall-clock token counters against client-side request counts.
- Aggregation edge effects: averaging many short spikes can inflate numbers. Always examine raw time-series and prefer contiguous stable windows.
- Thermal ramp down: throughput slowly declines after N minutes. Check GPU temperature trace aligned to throughput. If decline >5% over the stable window, mark run unstable.
- Queue thrash vs throughput: high queue depth with poor latency indicates overloaded scheduling. Inspect queue depth histogram correlated to latency spikes.

Minimal audit playbook (step-by-step):
1) Collect raw artifacts: request logs, server token counters, GPU telemetry (nvidia-smi / DCGM traces), client pacing logs, and harness orchestrator events.
2) Compute warmup boundary using the adaptive heuristic; drop warmup.
3) Run sliding-window variance analysis to select the stable 5-minute window.
4) Compute per-shard and global throughput for the window, produce p50/p95 latencies for same window.
5) Run three reproducibility checks (seed replay, concurrency +/-10%, jitter injection).
6) Produce an audit note with: selected window, reasons (plots), delta between peak/median/long-run, and whether thermal or queue issues were observed.

Quick diagnostics cheat-sheet (commands / queries):
- Sum tokens produced per GPU: (server token counter delta) / window_seconds.
- Client ingress rate: count(request_start events) / window_seconds.
- Queue depth correlation: compute correlation(queue_depth, p95_latency, window=30s).
- GPU thermal check: extract max temp in window and any throttle events from DCGM logs.

What to publish alongside claims:
- headline_throughput_window: e.g., "5m at 2024-12-01T14:20:00Z to 14:25:00Z"
- per_gpu_breakdown: CSV or table (gpu-id, tokens/s, p95 latency)
- artifacts: tarball path to raw traces & harness config
- reproducibility_summary: list of replays and deltas (seed1:+1.2%, seed2:-0.8%, jitter:-9.6%)

Open questions / TODOs (investigate in next cycle):
- Should our default stable window be 5m for very bursty workloads? Consider adaptive window length based on variance.
- Define formal threshold for "thermal instability" (>X% decline over Y minutes).
- Automate selection of stable window and artifact packaging for audit.

Appendix: example note template to include with any throughput claim (fill before sharing):
- Run id: <GUID>
- Model + config: <model, quant, kv_cache, max_seq>
- Harness version: <git sha>
- Cluster layout: <n gpus, type>
- Workload fingerprint: <tokens distribution, request shapes>
- Warmup policy used: <duration or adaptive>
- Stable window chosen: <start, end>
- Headline throughput: <tokens/s> (60s / 5m / 15m)
- Reproducibility summary: <3 replays with deltas>
- Observed issues: <thermal/queue/imbalance/clock-skew>
- Attached artifacts: <paths/links>

Notes to self: keep this doc concise; heavy instrumentation makes the audit convincing but also expensive. For quick stakeholders (sales / benchmarks) export only the headline numbers + a short reproducibility note. For infra/eng follow-ups attach raw traces.

End of note.
